newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish army pressures Islamist-led coalition.
newsitem.headline: Turkish army pressures Islamist-led coalition.

text.p: Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, his government barely clinging to power, came under renewed pressure on Saturday from Turkey's secularist armed forces to crack down against Moslem activism.

The army brass used the monthly meeting of the National Security Council (NSC) to assess Erbakan's implementation of earlier directives, issued back in February, to curb what it sees as mounting threats to Turkey's official secular order.

"Information was presented to the Council and an assessment was made about implementation of measures, outlined in the February 28 decision of the National Security Council, against Islamist activities," the NSC said in a brief statement.
"Peace and security across the country, affected by internal and external developments, were reviewed at the meeting," said the council, which met for more than five hours -- twice the alotted time.
Erbakan left the NSC meeting without talking to reporters.
The army, spearheading an attack by Turkey's traditional secularist elite, first challenged Erbakan to move against his own grassroots supporters at the Council's February meeting.
It issued an 18-point anti-Islamist package, including bans on traditional Moslem dress, sharp limitations on Koranic education for youngsters and restrictions on Islamist business and media.
So far Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, has dragged his feet, setting him at odds with his conservative and secularist coalition partners, the True Path Party of Tansu Ciller.
The result has been a steady flow of defections of True Path MPs and ministers -- all decrying Erbakan's failure to implement the army directives.

On Friday the resignation of a senior True Path deputy and former minister cost the government its absolute majority in parliament, leaving it one seat short of the 276 votes needed to win a confidence vote.

Later on Friday Erbakan held three hours of talks with Ciller but they were unable to agree on True Path proposals for Ciller to lead an "election government" to ease the political crisis and take the country to early polls.
Fresh talks between the two were expected soon in an effort the bridge the gap, and each leader huddled late on Saturday with their respective party elders to plot strategy.
Turkish press reports say Erbakan was pushing for a quick poll, with Ciller holding out for a date sometime next spring. Elections would normally be due by the year 2000.
However, a conservative minister suggested on Saturday that True Path might be prepared to support a snap election.
"We do not know the certain date but elections could take place in mid-October," state-run Anatolian news agency quoted Health Minister Ismail Karakuyu as saying.
"Elections will diminish the tension in the country," Karakuyu said.
Before the formal NSC meeting, Erbakan joined dignitaries at a ceremony to mark the council's founding in the 1930s.

The event appeared to be aimed at boosting the profile of the army, which has deposed three civilian governments in four decades, ahead of the monthly council meeting, which groups senior military and civilian leaders.

"Since the day it came to power, our government has given priority to the strategic issues recommended by the National Security Council and made an effort to put them into force," the prime minister said in a speech.
